Bass, the pretty cloak model of New York
who was arrested yesterday on the charge
of stealing horse and buggy, says her
arrest will prevent her marriage to a rich
young man next week. Who her prospective

up her wedding or not."

There is a lockout at the plant of
the Chicago Rockford Hosiery Com
pany and in keeping with the new law
to govern child labor the managers of
the big stocking manufacturing firm
have discharged all the children in the
factory under the age of fourteen
years. Thirty of the little boys and
girls who have been working at the
benches for some time have been fore
ed to give up their positions and the
parents will have to provide for their
support during the vacation months.
The discharging of the children has in
measure crippled some of the depart
ments of the factory but as soon as
possible the places of the children will
be filled with older boys and girls and
in the end the factory will benefit by
the change.


Manager w. w. Cooper is complete
ly in harmony with the new law and
in commenting on the matter this
morning he said: "Of course the dis
charge of these children has crippled
us little but the law is proper one
and we are glad to aid in its enforce
ment. All the children working with
us had permits and many of them
were taken under urgent pleas from
the parents who depend on them for
support. In some cases these slittle
fellows we're earning four dollars a
week and their earnings IN several
cases we're the sole support of mothers
and fathers. The demands for the en-
ployment of children in Kenosha are
very numerous and often times, even
if we would prefer not to have the
little fellows about, these demands
force US to take them into the factories
in order that they may assist in support
ing the families. The law is good one
and it's enforcement will better the
conditions of labor in the stated


The example of the Hosiery Works
ia releasing the children will undoubt-
eddy be followed by all the other fac
tories where the smaller children are
employed and IN another week it is
not expected that child under the
legal age will be at work in any of the
factories of the city.


Judge Slosson of the County Court
has formally notified the managers of
the different factories that under his
construction of the law the children
now working in violation of the law
must leave the factories and it is prob
able that this announcement will be
sufficient to secure compliance from
the factory managers without carry
ing the matter into any of the courts
of the county.

nopah. Mr.. Peters was born in OF

st. Michaels, having navigated the Yu-

returned to San Francisco on three
masted schooner. While his Alaskan

great deal of attention. One year in

mining propositions in southern Ore
gon, Mr. Peters landed in San Fran

coy flirt and leads most unexpectedly

Being in the mining bureau at San
Francisco he accidentally picked up a
Virginia City Enterprise and read a
three line item about Tonopah. This
was in December, 1900. The item

War Eagle In Copper.


The navy annex building, just west
of the War Department building on
Pennsylvania avenue, Washington, D.C.,
is surmounted by one of the most elaborate eagles to be seen on any government flagstaff. It is a facsimile in
copper and aluminium of the famous
Bald Eagle "Old Abe" which
the Eighth Wisconsin Volunteers carried with them through the Civil war
and for many years maintained its
principal quarters at the capital in
Madison.


The Eighth was raised in the
"Pimys" in the northern part of
the state, and consisted for the most part
of short-haired lumbermen fresh from
the woods, one of them brought into
camp a young eagle which he had
caught and kept as a pet in the home.
The boys adopted it as the mascot of the regiment at once, and a standard was made for it.


Wherever the regiment marched
the eagle went along. It was named
after President Lincoln. When the
Eighth left Wisconsin for the front,
the regiment experienced a good deal
of hard fighting and "Old Abe" went
through it all once or twice, sometimes
his feathers chipped by bullets in
battle. He frequently won his perch on
the standard, and flew scimitar-
like over the heads of the men. He was
carried by a huge Swede, who always
walked side by side with the color
bearer of the regiment.


The copper and aluminium eagle on
the navy annex building measures
ninety-six inches from tip to tip of
his outstretched wings. His head
and tail feathers are white and shine
in the sunshine like furnished silver.
The big bird sits on top of a tall iron post that rises above the street and is very visible from a distance.


Owing to its pivotal arrangement,
it always faces the wind, and in this
way its shape is perfect. Many say the
bird is a symbol of freedom to remind men conspicuous on its elevated perch of

based on cowardice and is a prolific cause of

Former Attorney General Taylor deserves
credit for speaking strongly on this subject
before the State Bar Association and for
proposing a remedy. His proposition, by the
way, was conspicuous for being the only
practical suggestion made at the meeting
for the suppression or diminution of crime.

regulate the sale Of pistols and to declare

person not clearly authorized by law to car

There is no law in Indiana making pistols
contraband when found in the pockets of
highwaymen. There is no authority for
their destruction. The sandbagger is caught
with a pistol in his pocket, and if fined the
pistol must be handed back to him for fur
Their use. If he is sent to prison the pistol,
ebony-handled and glistening from use. Is
sold to the boy for use again. From three
TO five hundred pistols a year are taken
from the pockets of men arrested in this
city. There is now an armory OF two hum
dred pistols at the police station. Yet under
the law there is no power to declare them
contraband. They are put up at auction and
sold for a trifie to be used again, and thus
we go round and round.


The law might go even further than Mr..
Taylor suggests. 1t might not only regu-
late the sale of pistols and declare them
contraband when found in unauthorized
hands. but it might require every purchaser
of a pistol to be registered and to pay an
annual license or tax for the privilege of
carrying it. Whatever would tend to make
the purchase, ownership or carrying Of a
pistol difficult or expensive would be in the
direction of reform.


The pistol-carrying practice is doubly vi
cious, first because it is cowardly and de-
moralizing in itself, and second, because it
is q violation of law. 1t is the main cause
of most of the murders and homicides that
occur in the State and a contributing cause

the continuance should be granted, as

of the law, in the service of the minor in this case, is against the father. It was culpable in eyes of the law, because it lacked consent. The father's consent to the minor's service is condition precedent to the enforcement of any status against the parent. Without that consent, this minor was of the class forbidden to serve, under the very terms of the law, as emphatically as any other minor who is forbidden to serve, and cannot acquire any military status; for he was debarred as against the father from entering into the new relation. As I said in People v. Warden, 100 N. Y. 20, this requirement is, therefore, made the condition of a valid enlistment. The right not to consent, is a weapon the law furnishes the parent to destroy the Government's claim. It is the right to take off the uniform, and all its wearing implements. The father here is the wronged party, and the Government the wrongdoer. The father can take advantage of the lack of qualification. As against him, the Government could not waive it, or create any right against him by trying to waive it. The language of the opinion "the mother not interfering, he was bound to remain in the service" inevitably implies if the parent had interfered, the minor would not be bound to remain. "If he would not be bound" leaving the service was not desertion. The interference puts an end to the service, as to the father, and destroyed the only status which could authorize the military authority to detain the body of the minor from the custody of the parent.

Finally, it is urged that the privileges of the writ should not be awarded, here until the minor has been punished for assertion; because it would initiate against the maintenance of discipline in the navy. Winthrop, in his admirable work on Military Law and Precedents, Vol. 2, p. 549, speaking of this matter says: "In such an instance, the claims of the private individual—the parents—are deemed to be subordinated to the interest of the public, in the due administration of justice, and maintenance of military discipline, and the minor soldier is, therefore, required to abide by and undergo the legitimate consequences of his own wrong, before any petition for his discharge from his contract can be entertained." But is it only the claim of private individual, which is here involved? Is not the right of every parent to the custody of his minor child, secured and protected by the common law and statutes of the State and enforced in the statutes of the United States, involved in the rights of the private individual now before the court? If his rights must be subordinated, so must the rights of every one of the millions of parents in this land. The matter is one of the highest public concern, in comparison with which the insignificance of the individual or his inconvenience sinks out of sight. It is a case where the invasion of the rights of one is the concern of all.

The law of the States and the United States protects these rights and the question, therefore, concerns not only the State and Federal Governments but all the people of these United States. Who determines what is "the interest of the public"? What are the sources to which we must go, to ascertain what is public policy and what it requires? We must seek the will of the people, as embodied in the law of the land. The enlistment statute declares what is the interest of the public in this instance. The minor's wrong is not the vital matter. It is the government's wrong to the father, in holding the minor against his wishes, which constitutes the substance of the controversy, which the court is invoked to redress.

The awarding of the privileges of the writ, if the father has any rights in this matter, is mandatory and compulsory, and not of grace. If the right claimed is well founded, the court on every consideration of law and justice, must take the law as it finds it and shut its eyes to the consequences of fearlessly enforcing it. Considerations of policy must therefore, be without legitimate influence in determining whether the privileges of the writ should be granted here. If, however, awarding the privileges of the writ here, were discretionary, it would be the bounden duty of the court to give heed to the vital importance of maintaining discipline in the millions of homes in this land, as well as to the effect upon discipline in the navy. If the influence and control of fathers and mothers can be successfully set at naught, by the government, because of unlawful dealings with their minor children, in the teeth of solemn enactments of Congress, a spectacle will be presented to the youth of the country, destructive of respect for authority in the home, which is so essential to the formation of character and getting the youth for future service to the country, whether as civilians or soldiers. Such a state of things, as said by Chief Justice Shaw in Commonwealth v. Downes, 24 Pick. 10, would lead to a state of society very much like an anarchy. The cultivation of civic virtues and the discipline of restraint and respect for authority, can nowhere be better taught than around the hearthstone. It is the nursery from which must spring the training which fits free people for self-government, without which, their institutions are weak, regardless of the strength of their armies or navies. In view of these considerations, which at every period in the history of our country seem to have controlled the legislation regarding the enlistment of minors, it is difficult to defend the theory, in the teeth of this statute, that where invasion of the parental right was involved, Congress intended to deny its full enforcement, because of the collateral disturbance.

Mr. White says there is absolutely no question in his mind that the two scientists contributed at least $15 to the Indians in connection with their dance. He makes the assertion on the authority of the assistant clerk in his office, who says he saw the money passed. He explains, however, that the money was ostensibly given for the lariat to which slaughtered beef, and for the stick which was thrust under the flesh of a tortured Indian.

More startling than this is his statement that after the dance and after the torture the scientists paid one of the tortured Indians money for the piece of skin that was torn from his back in the course of the ordeal.

He also says that two Indians and not one were subjected to the torture, and when asked to explain the nature of their part in the program he said:

The camp of the Indians was arranged in the shape of a horse shoe. The Indian selected for the torture barred his back, and two parallel slits were made just back of and below about three inches long. A knife blade was then thrust into the back from slit to slit, and through the hole thus made a stick was thrust. The lariat led out from the back for a few feet and then the ends were knotted together.

At the knot one end of a single strand of the lariat was tied, and at the other end of it the gruesome head of freshly slaughtered beef was attached. In the published reports which I have seen on the incident reference is made to buffalo head. There were no buffaloes in the southwest procurable for this or any other purpose.

He is convinced, however, that the tortured Indian was either Yellow Leggins or Wolf Belly.

ST. Petersburg, December 20.—Private letters
from Rostov on the Don, conveying the information
that the strike there is not confined to the state rail
road shops, but affects equally many private work
shops and factories. The political character of this
strike has not been concealed from the beginning.

in large part the same the students have popu-
larized, namely personal freedom, freedom of

meeting. The men also demand shorter work day,
more pay, more tolerable shop rules, etc.

During the recent gatherings at Rostov it is re-
ported that from 10,000 to 40,000 persons assembled
in the streets and that revolutionary speeches were
made. The Cossacks were called in to break up the
meeting. The first time they advanced on the crowd
the people lay down upon the ground before the ad-
vancing cavalry. The Cossacks' horses veered at
this unexpected spectacle and the soldiers were in-
able to use their leaden-tipped whips to advantage.

women, who were arrested in Saratov last May for
participating in strike demonstration in honor of
Balmashev the assassin of Alexander II, all the
accused admitted that they participated in the scene
intentionally and they boldly defended their course
on political grounds. The women prisoners were
medical students practising physicians assistants.
The trial has been concluded but the sentences have
not yet been announced.

mothers they are as big as half
grown lambs.


I know many an old hunter who
not only will not kill she bears that
have cubs; but will take every meas-
ure to protect them. This is from
no prompting of humanity, however;
it is simply with an eye out for the
main chance in the future, when
those cubs have grown to bears, fat
and in fine fur.


"A motherless bear cub is poor
property, and a bear mother nurs-
ing her young is of no use either as
meat or for fur. But her cubs in
year will be worth from $40 to $15
apiece, and she will herself be worth
more than that by the time she is
ready to hole up the next winter.


It is not an uncommon thing for
bears to have four cubs at birth.
I have heard of five at a birth. Three
are common, two more common, but
one may be counted on as being the
most common.


The instance of five bear cubs at
birth I can't vouch for from per-
sonal knowledge, although I saw the
old bear, and the man who killed her
had five cubs, which he declared were
all with her when he shot her. The
man was known as a person of we-
racity, but I have my own ideas
about a man who could find it in his
heart to kill a bear that had five
helpless little cubs at her side. But
that doesn't make him out a liar.


I have personal knowledge, nev-
ertheless, of a bear that had eight
cubs with her when I came across
her in the woods, and she was rear-
ing them with motherly ten-
derness. That was after I had heard
of the one with five cubs, and I felt
that I had come to a conclusion too
hasty as to the veracity of the man
who had exhibited them.


"This bear with eight cubs was
such an extraordinary and unheard-
of thing that I resolved to capture
the whole family alive if I could.
When the old bear saw me she with-
drew, with a great show of fierce-
ness, to the refuge of fallen tree
top, hustling the cubs along in ad-
vance of her.


While reconnoitering to see how it
might be possible for me to carry
out my designs on the bear fairly, I
stumbled over a dead bear only a
few rods from where the other one
and the eight cubs had their quar-

had her cubs.

but I thought I had a clear explana-
tion of the other bear's remarkable
family. She had four cubs of her
own, and, having come across the
orphaned cubs whining on the dead
body of their mother, she had adopt-
ed them and was rearing them with
her own. I made no further effort
to capture that bear family, and the
live she lived undoubtedly dined on
them. I searched the dead mother of her
four cubs.


"It is about fawns and
their mothers. A fawn when first
born is for some hours unable to
stand. The doe does not remain be-
side it, but paces slowly around at a
considerable distance.


Every little while she gives a trem-
ulous, low, bleating call. At the
sound the fawn lifts its head and
tries to struggle to its feet.


Should the doe scent danger, such
as the approach of some one in the
woods, she runs away in a straight
line, but flaggingly and haltingly, as
though she were badly hurt. When
she is satisfied that she has turned
the enemy far enough away, she
gives three great flying leaps, which
quickly take her out of sight, and
she returns speedily to her helpless
young.


"If she is not disturbed she keeps
up the pacing about and the bleating
until she sees the fawn able to rise
and keep its feet. Then she prances
daintily away in a straight line,
choosing always the easiest thorough-
fare.

ping every few yards to look over
her shoulder to see that the fawn is
following. She conducts the little
one to a hiding place, and she can
and does hide her fawn from sight,
although one may be almost upon
it, as absolutely as the hen pheasant
clucks her brood into concealment at
a sign of danger."

"Hide?" he said, looking at the flower but not at her.

"I trust you kept the rose, Monsieur Diplomat?" she spoke up, suddenly, her expression most serious.

This, then, was the information she had taken such a roundabout way to communicate; it was to this end she had purposely led the conversation by adroit stages, studying him gaily, impatiently or maliciously, she marked the effect of her words upon him. All alive, she stepped back laughing; elated, she put her arms about a branch of the rose bush and drew score of roses to her bosom, as though she were, "I'm impervious to thorns." He had risen—yes, there was no doubt about it.—but her sunny face was turned to the flowers. His countenance became at once puzzled and thoughtful.

"The duke—coming—" he condescended to ask for information now.

Sidewise she gazed at him, unreticent. "Does the flower become me?" she asked.

"The duke—coming—" he repeated.

"How impolite to refuse me compliment," she flashed.

The next moment he was by her side, and had taken her arm, almost roughly.

"Speak out!" he cried; "Someone is coming!"

"You hurt me—" she exclaimed, angrily. He loosened his grasp.

"What duke?" she answered, scornfully. "Her duke! Your duke! The Emperor's duke!"

"The Duke of Friedwald?" he asked.

"Of course. The princess's fiance; bridegroom-to-be; future husband, lord and master," she explained, with indubious and positive iteration.

"But the time—set for the wedding—has not expired," he protested, with what she thought seemed suspicion that she was playing with him.

"That is easily answered," she said cheerfully. "The duke, it seems, has become more and more enamored. Finally his passion has so grown and grown he fears to let it grow any more, and, as the only way out of the difficulty, petitioned the King to cut off the constantly augmenting suspense. To which his most gracious Majesty, having been a lover himself on divers occasions, by the qualms he has himself experienced, has seen generously fit to cut off a few weeks of waiting and set the wedding for the near future."

"How know you this?" he demanded, sharply, striding to and fro.

"This morning the princess sent me with a message to the Countess d'Etampes. You know her? You have heard? She has succeeded the Countess of Chateaubriant. Well, the King was with her—not the Countess of Chateaubriant, but the other one, I mean. They left poor me to await his Majesty's pleasure, and, as the Countess d'Etampes has but newly succeeded to her present exalted position and the King has not yet discovered her many imperfections, I should certainly have fallen asleep for weakness had I not CHANGED TO overhear portions of their conversation. The Countess d'Etampes, it seemed, was very angry. 'Your Majesty!' But, my dear, give me time, pleaded the King. 'Pack her off at once!' she demanded, raising her voice. 'Send her to her husband. That's where she belongs. Think of him, poor fellow!' Laughing, his Majesty capitulated. 'Well, well, back to her castle goes the Countess of Chateaubriant!'" Thereupon—

"But the duke, mistress?" interrupted the jester, who had become more and more impatient during the prolonged narration.

"Can I not tell it in my own way?" she returned. "What manners you have. First you pinch my arm until I must needs fly out, then you ask so and so and interrupt!" he muttered. "You might have told a dozen tales. What care I for the King's Jezebels?"

"I see plainly. If you don't die one way you—"

"'Tis usually the case. But go on with your story."

"If I cannot tell it in my own way—"

"Tell it as you will. If your way be as slow as your tongue is sharp," he answered, sulky.

"Sharp! Jezebels! You deserve not to hear, but—the King, it seems, had laid the duke's request before the Countess d'Etampes. 'Here is an impatient suitor,' he said gaily. 'How shall we cure his passion?' 'By marrying him,'blithely answered this light-of-love. 'Tis a medicine that never fails.' His Majesty frowned; I could not see him, but felt sure of it from his tone, for, although he neglects the Queen, yet, to some degree, is mindful of her dignity. 'Marriage is a holy state, madam,' he replied severely. 'There's no doubt about it, Francis,' returned the lady, 'and therefore is the antidote to passion. But man bent on matrimony is like a child that wants a toy. Better give it to him at once.' 'Nay, madam,' he said reprovingly, 'the duke shall have his wish, but for no such reason.' 'What reason then?' quoth she petulantly. 'Because thou hast shown me love is a monarch stronger than any king and that we are but as slaves in its hands,' he exclaimed, passionately. 'I shall like the duke,' cried she, 'since he is the cause of that pretty speech!'"

"At this point, not daring to listen longer, I coughed; there was silence. Then the countess herself appeared at the door and I could command. I delivered my message, left the house and was hurrying through the garden where chance threw you in my way; and now you have it all, sir."

"The princess—has she heard the King has received a letter from the duke, and that his Majesty has changed the wedding date?" The jester spoke slowly, but Jacqueline was assured that beneath his deliberate manner surged deep and conflicting emotions; that his calmness was no more than a mask to conceal his pain. Had he given utterance to the feeling that beset him, had he betrayed more than a suggestion of the passion, rage or grief which struggles for mastery beneath a forced sloth of sensibility, she would have once more knocked him with laughter. But perhaps his very quiescence inclined her to look upon him with a grain of sympathy or compassion, for her tones were now grave.

"The princess knows; has heard all from the court. 'Is the court, then, only mart, a guild hall?' he exclaimed. 'A woman—even a princess—should be won, not exchanged.'"

Her lashes dropped. In her gaze shone once more their ironical amusement. "Why," she said, "from what wilds or forests have you come? Do you mean that she—"

"I mean that her welfare is in strong hands; that there will be few greater in all the land: none more honored! The duke's principality is vast—but here comes the princess!" The hound sprang to his feet and ran gamboling down the path. "Ask her the rest yourself, most unsophisticated fool, what handsome bride she will make for the duke!"

election, as well as that of Sheriff
Callahan, was protested by James B.
Marcum of Jackson. Callahan was
Hargis's brother-in-law. Dr. Cox
openly expressed his participation in
the protest and for this offense was
shot and killed.

But other victims were soon to be
sacrificed to the resentment of the
Hargis faction. Curtis Jett shot
and killed John Cockrell. Not long
afterward James B. Marcum was shot
and killed in the court house at Jackson. Curtis Jett and Thomas White
are now serving life sentences for
committing this crime, which has
brought the Cockrell-Hargis feud
prominently into notice.

It has taken so many years of this sort of
strife to deaden the moral sense of
Breckitt county to the lawlessness
that the Cockrell and Hargis differences have brought about. Those on
either side who have become attached
to the one or the other have learned
to regard the feud as a matter quite
outside of the law, a matter to be settled, as their own private affair, between the two families. It does not
appear that at any time an arbitrator has arisen, moved by a spirit of
peace and longing for murder to bring
about an agreement to settle the vendetta that can only be terminated, if
a pacific settlement is not reached, by
the death of the last male survivor of
one of the families.

Yet these people move with apparent unconcern about the streets and
along the roads, the children sometimes attend the same school, and
Cockrells and Hargises have been
known to gather in the same
churches. But the poison is moving
in the blood all the time.

The shooting of young John
McLaurin, Of Bogue Chitto, by
Charles ?. Tapley, Of jackson, in
one of the west side resorts last
Saturday night is surrounded with
many sad features. In the hos
pital the victim of Tapley's bull
let lies quiet as death, his face and
pulseless hand, white as the down
of pillows bolstering him up, so
he can breathe. He pays little
heed to those surrounding him
and patiently bears the pain of the
wound that may yet demand the
forfeit of his young life. Nc
Laurin is but a lad. He is under
seventeen and in many homes he
would be loved and petted like
child. He is motherless, father
less and without relative in the
wide world, save a cousin and
step-mother. This step-mother
has shielded him as her own; has
sought to guide his steps and
mould his ambitions, that a noble
and wise career might ensue.
Prayerful and loving has been the
counsel, but like many other boys,
McLaurin, though his native dis
position is sweet, tractable and
generous, is easily led when in
crowd of boys who are his seniors.


This was the case Saturday
night when he met the bullet that
is laying siege to the citadel of
life. He left Bogue Chitto with
several young bloods-thec blue
bloods'' Of the town-and by ar
Iangement they met other ''bIue
bloodso who are students at Mill
saps, and the crowd set out to do
the town proper. 1t may not be
the lack of home training or low
ing, wise mothers that boys will
run it to evil; simply runs in the
veins of youth. The fire burns
and to control its devouring
flames is to become manful and
self-masterful. 'He that ruleth
his own spirit is greater than he
that taketh city," To give way
to the cracking demands means
God alone knows what. The
rich iron, the strong bounding
tonic of youth becomes more
stimulated through the poison of
tobacco or alcohol; and these
habits, like a demon from hell,
drive the awakened passions of
the person thus crazed, lead the
young bound. Kindness a n d
charity should cover the misdeeds
of youth. Life's lessons are hard
to learn and harder to forget.


But these outward outbreakings
simply suggest several things
worthy of consideration. / have
no word of censure for young
Tapley. He is a man in years and
experience. He comes from
home of responsibility and love.
He has disgraced the mother
whose pure lips first kissed him

Washington, D.C.—The Secretary of the Navy has before him for action charges involving two Rear Admirals, which, however, will be adjusted without reference to court-martial. The officers concerned are Rear-Admiral Robert Y. Evans, Communicating Chief of the Asiatic Station, and Rear-Admiral Albert Kenney, Paymaster-General of the Navy. Admiral Evans began the trouble by bringing charges against Admiral Kenney, who has retaliated with counter charges against Admiral Evans.

The difficulty between these two high ranking officers is the result of an alleged misunderstanding of an order issued by the Navy Department in regard to changes in the equipment and clothing of persons in the service. Upon the receipt of the order by Admiral Evans he made formal requisition on the Navy Department for the necessary material to put into effect the changes required. The requisition was met with resistance by the Bureau of Supplies and Accounts, of which Admiral Kenney is the Chief. Admiral Kenney returned in communication to Admiral Evans with the statement that such an immediate and wholesale change in uniforms as that contemplated was contrary to the interests of the Government, and Admiral Evans was informed that if his intention was approved the Government would have upon its hands a large amount of old material which it was desirable to use before the new material was drawn upon.

Admiral Evans then wrote to Secretary Moody, saying that Admiral Kenney had not only exceeded his authority, but had been disrespectful to another officer. He charged also that Admiral Kenney had attacked the Secretary of the Navy by questioning the wisdom of the order issued by the Department.

Admiral Evans's allegations were referred to the Bureau of Navigation, which made an endorsement favorable to the attitude of Paymaster-General Kenney, to whom the papers were sent for comment and explanation. Admiral Kenney replied by charging that the communication from Admiral Evans contained statements in violation of the naval regulations, in that they reflected upon the Paymaster-General. He alleged also that Admiral Evans was guilty of misconduct in failing to furnish the Paymaster-General with copy of the charges, a requirement which Admiral Kenney did not overlook in his own accusations against Admiral Evans, by mailing a copy of them to that officer, duly certified and otherwise put into official form.

There has been voluminous correspondence, which Secretary Moody now has on his desk. It is said, however, that he will ignore the charges and counter-charges and merely file them in the Department records. Admiral Kenney will reach the retiring age this month, but on Secretary Moody's recommendation the President has decided to retain him on active duty until the expiration of the term of four years, in which he was commissioned as Paymaster-General in May, 1880.

for consumption and expectation,
that land which yields three or four
harvests year, is not earth at all,
but pure, clean sand. It is ceaselessly
expelled by the turbulent ocean, is
whirled away by the furious western
winds, and scattered all over the dis-
trict of Rota, like the ashes in the
vicinity of Vesuvius.

But the incessant toil of man more
than compensates for the ingratitude
of Nature. I do not believe that in all
the world there is a laboring man
who toils so much as the Rotanese.
Not even a tiny stream of sweet
water flows through those melan-
choly fields. What does it matter?
The pumpkin-raiser perforates his

draws out here by hand, there by
buckets—the precious fluid which
serves as blood to the vegetables. The
principles of fertilization are also
wanting in sand. What does it mat-
ter? The tomato-raiser passes half
his life seeking and removing sub-
stances which will serve as guano,
converting even the sea-weeds into
manure! Once possessed of these two
precious elements, the son of Rota
proceeds patiently to fertilize not his
entire estate, but little circles of
ground as large as a small plate; in
each of these fertilized circles he
sows a grain of tomato or pumpkin
seed, which he then waters from
a small jar, just as one would give a
drink to a little child.

From the time of planting until the
harvest, he tends the plants daily, one
by one, treating them with the fond-
ness and pains comparable only to
the solicitude of a spinster for her
flower-pots. Now he adds a little
handful of manure; now he pours on
a little stream of water; now he
clears them of caterpillars and other
insects; now he cares for the infirm,
splinting the fractures and placing
bulwarks of sand and straw beside
those which cannot resist the rays of
the sun or the blasts of the wind. He
counts the stems, the leaves, the
flowers and the fruit of the most
precious, and talks to them, kisses
them, blesses them, and even gives
them expressive names to distinguish
them in his mind.

ready a saying (and I have heard it
many times in Rota) that the garden-
er of that country touches no less
than 40 times with his own hand
every single plant which he raises in
his garden. And this explains why
the old gardeners of that locality go
about bent double, until their boards
touch their knees. It is the posture
in which they have spent their noble,
meritorious lives.

System of Improvement

In improving some sections of the upper river the work has been done by means of shore protection, dams and wing dams, constructed of brush and stone, which are found in abundance on the banks of the river.

By this method of improvement the side channels are closed in, which are termed closing dams, thus limiting the low water flow to one channel. One bank of this channel is usually protected from caving by revetment and the river contracted by the construction of wing dams on the opposite shore. The width of the navigation varies from St. Paul to the mouth of the Missouri in accordance with the low water discharge of the river at different places. At St. Paul the prescribed width of the river is 400 feet; at the mouth of St. Croix it widens to 600 feet; at Lake Pepin it is 800 feet; below the mouth of the Wisconsin river 1,000 feet; at Quincy, 1,200 feet; from the Illinois river to the mouth of the Missouri, 1,000 feet.

The expenditures since 1874 have failed to meet the requirements of the people engaged in the navigation of the river and in commercial and industrial enterprises in the upper Mississippi valley. The only part of the river that has been thoroughly improved is a short piece extending from St. Paul to Red Wing, Minn. Above Lake Pepin the river is a broad sheet of water and occupies the entire valley from bluff to bluff. In that part of the river the improvement works are almost continuous and the results obtained have been very successful. While the river there is smallest in volume than any place in its course and the channel is only 300 feet wide, there is a continuous good channel the year round, better, in fact, than is sometimes found between Cairo and St. Louis, after the river has received the tributaries of 700 miles of its course, including the Missouri, which is as large as the Mississippi itself. So far the work has been very local in character; improvements have been made principally at places where experience has shown they were needed most. Improved places are often discomfited by miles of unimproved river, and at the unimproved places sandbars develop which give trouble at the low water season.

Plea for Reservoir System.

The people near the headwaters, particularly in St. Paul and Minneapolis, are urging an enlargement of the reservoir system, but this plan does not receive much consideration at the hands of engineers, who claim that the natural reservoir is Lake Pepin and that it is adequate.

The most radical element among river improvement promoters was the ultimate development of the river to twelve feet. This would necessitate, according to the engineers, the building of movable dams similar to those on the Ohio River. The most optimistic see with the eyes of faith a time when the headwaters of the river might be connected with Lake Superior, furnishing a water outlet in a practically straight line from the Great Lakes to the isthmian canal, but this idea has no place in the present scheme of development.

Des Moines, Sept. 18.—The preparation of the biennial report of the state board of control is now going on and the report will be presented to the governor and be printed before the time for the legislature to take up the work of considering the state institutions. One of the minor duties of the board about which there has been some controversy in the past has just been taken up. This is the examination of the state educational institutions. Judge Robinson, of the board, and A. S. Gown, the accountant, are in Council Falls making investigation into the accounts of the state normal school. Later the state university and the state college will be visited. The law providing for the board of control requires that the board shall make examination of the affairs of these three institutions, and specifically requires that the board shall inquire whether there has been a faithful accounting of the money received from appropriations or otherwise, and as to whether or not persons have received per diem and mileage other than legal, and into the manner of letting contracts, and whether or not the institutions are conducted in an economical and businesslike manner, etc. The scope of the investigation is wide. At the outset the members of the board on organizing felt that this extension of their duties was a semi-supervision over the finances of the educational institutions was superfluous and that it was a mistake to require the board to report on matters over which it has no control. Whatever, but there was the law and the board had naught to do but comply, hence an investigation was made two years ago this month and another is being made now. It was over the reports made two years ago that great noise and cry was raised that the board of control was trying to decry the work of the trustees of the educational institutions. It was said the board wanted to be given charge of these institutions. This was not the case, but it served the purpose of those who desired a sensation for time. It was also declared that as a result of the criticisms made by the board in the line of its plain duty, and upon the evidence as furnished at the educational institutions, there would be a change in the law. But the law was allowed to remain unchanged. Now there will be much interest in the next report for comparison with the last and to determine whether or not the suggestions made by the board have been considered or acted upon.


In the report on the state normal school two years ago the state board found much to commend and some things to criticise. We found, said the board, "that the persons holding positions had faithfully accounted for all moneys drawn from the state treasury, as well as all other moneys that had come into their hands as such officers, and that all appropriations had been drawn in accordance with law." While this general commendation was made it was pointed out that on one occasion there was $50 paid out of the general contingent fund to assist students in defraying expenses in the alumni association, and that the institution purchased 125 banquet tickets at $1 each for an alumni banquet; that while an auditing committee generally approved all vouchers it was found that fifteen had been paid without being found to be unsigned by the president; that on one occasion the building fund was illegally overdrawn $1,799; that on another occasion the military drill fund was overdrawn a small amount; that the trustees had improperly paid the secretary $500 a year for services as bookkeeper, which services belonged to the position of secretary; and that not in all cases were the contracts for buildings written, but consisted of mere acceptances of bids. The board recommended the employment of a secretary who should be paid a fair salary and have an office in the college and handle all the business. The reports on the State University and the State College were of similar character and merely pointed out those little defects of management which were handed down from past generations and have never been rectified.


At the conference of the superintendents this week an interesting discussion came up on a paper by Superintendent McCune, of the College for the Blind, over the question of the proper housing of the superintendents and officers of the various institutions. Superintendent McCune took the ground that superintendent should live outside of the institution, that there is refreshment and inspiration in getting away from the cares of the institution, that there should be some opportunity for a superintendent for home and social life without being subjected to criticism, and that he is entitled to the relaxation which can come only by getting clear away from the institution. Chairman Cownie, in discussing the same matter, said that he had formerly held this view, but now believed that the place for all officers and superintendents is right in the institution, where they may be ready for any emergency. peaceably over a piece of road outside
of an enclosure, either on foot or
horseback, at any rate we had Mr.
Wagner's permission to pass through
the gate in question.


Now, Mr. Robinson claims that
parties, by mistake drove into his
field over clover, potatoes and grain,
and that to get rid of that nuisance,
he posted up that notice. I would
simply say that he cannot cite one
single instance of that kind. If that
was his reason why did he not post
that notice on the gate that leads into
his field? Instead of that he posted
his notice on the road that runs out
side of his field, and why did they try
to stop me by force from travelling the
road outside of the fence?


Again, he says he did some slashing
preparatory to enlarging his field.
Now, the only slashing made consists
of a few fir trees felled in the road at
right angles or across it, apparently
for no other purpose but to obstruct
the road. Now, Mr. Robinson's only
purpose in trying to stop travel on
this road was to make us go around,
thus compelling us to travel two
miles further every day in order to
get to and from our work.


In regard to what occurred at the
gate in question, it is located at least
go rods from where they were making
hay, and they had to go some distance
out of their way to get to it. When
I arrived at the gate I found Mr.
Gland C. Robinson and his brother
Luther R. apparently waiting for me.
Mr. Robinson says they had wired
the gate, which is correct. They had
pitchfork standing short distance
away. They ordered me not to come
through the gate, but to go back from
whence I came. I paid no attention
to them and stopped down to unwire
the gate, where Gland C. immediately
assaulted me, trying to get hold of
my hand and arm, tearing away part
of the clothing. I then raised up and
pulled him away, when he struck me.
I then struck him in self-defense,
which ended the battle on rather short
notice, for he immediately broke
away and ran for the pitchfork and
returned with it to the gate. I then
broke the wire on the gate and passed
through. Both of my assailants then
ran back along the road to where they
had felled the trees across the road,
and there they took their stand, fork
in hand.


Now in regard to the tongue lashing,
I simply told them what I thought of
people who committed such acts.


Now, as well known in this part
of Josephine county, having travelled
for three years as Methodist preach
er in this part of the country, I have
never imposed on anyone. I have
always tried to do unto others as
I would have them do unto me, and
this senseless attack of these parties
on my person and my character, is a
most disagreeable thing, and cannot
be too strongly condemned by the pub
lic. Mr. Editor, your correspondent
told the truth. If people do not wish
to be called scoundrels, then let them
remain within the bounds of truth
and righteousness.


Very respectfully

I GANG

The Washington supper held by the
Ladies' Aid Society of the Grand Ave-
nue Congregational church on Wednes-
day evening was a great success. An
unusually fine supper was served to
about sixty patrons.

Three church suppers were served
last evening, viz., at St. James and
Grace Episcopal churches and at the East
Pearl Street Episcopal church.

Attorney Harry W. Asher sent word
yesterday that he would be unable to
deliver the address at Strong school on
the occasion of the Washington cele-
bration to be held next Tuesday after-
noon at o'clock in Granniss' hall, and
Principal Graves has secured the ser-
vices of Principal J. G. Knowlton, of
the Winchester district, who will deliv-
er the address.

Postmaster Howarth has had new
cards of directions placed on the front
side of the letter boxes in this vicinity,
which will be appreciated by patrons of
the mail service.

There was a runaway on Grand Ave.
which for a time
caused no little excitement. A horse
attached to a delivery sleigh owned by
H. R. Smith, frightened by a trolley
car, ran away and in front of Fl. E.
loves the sleigh struck a stone post.

but were not injured. The horse broke
away from the sleigh, but was soon
stopped. The damage caused was the
breaking of one of the runners to the
sleigh.

The gang of snow shovelers with
teams removed a great amount of snow
from Grand avenue yesterday. At
evening the surplus snow had been
cleared as far east as Ferry street.

The crew of a Montowese car blocked
near that place had to remain for two
hours and also report that their friends in the vicinity
provided them with food and sent
banquets for them to sleep in. The crews of
two vestibule cars stalled at Branford
had to remain an equal length of time
and also report kind attentions from
the Branford people.

With a temperature of one degree be-
low zero the weather yesterday was
cold enough even for the ice man. The
weather warmed up little towards
noon and the day was not as uncom-
portable as Wednesday. But it was
pretty cold for all that, especially on
the shady side of the street and in the
wake of the west wind.

car house in Fair Haven on Wednes-
day accomplished considerable in the
way of digging out the blockaded car
routes. The cars were running to East

green and the two big vestibule cars
were released and brought back to the
car house. The Branford cars were
running as usual yesterday and so were
the Montowese cars. The company has
had a pretty severe tussle with the
storm and it has cost it thousands of
dollars.

Total cross-cut tunnel run in two

Work on the cross-cut tunnel has
continued in extremely hard formation
for the last rs feet, the rock proving so
refractory that with our utmost efforts
we have at times almost despaired of
being able to penetrate it. Our New
Ingersoll drill, which represents the
highest efficiency of piston drill, was
unable to meet the requirements in the
hard rock. so we made test of the
new Model Water Leyner drill. Upon
securing proper equipment for operat-
ing this drill, we believe that we will be
enabled to secure greater efficiency and
at reduced expense.


The high footage cost shown by the
last two months work is explained by
the increasing difficulty in dealing with
rock of extreme hardness, at a con-
siderable distance under ground; the
greater distance required to tram the
waste causing an increase of faotage
cost.


The superintendent reports that the
last shifts, operating with the Leyner
drill, made encouraging progress,
owing to the higher efficiency of the
drills and the improving character of
the rock, which in the last eight feet
has become lighter and more easily
worked.


The consensus of opinion among
miners here is that the hard reef of
quartzite just passed through is an en-
couraging indication, and that good
values should exist back of such a
formation, The appearance of the
rock in the last eight feet shows the
laminations of such trend as to indi-
cate the approach to ledge. The
same conclusions may be derived from
the increasing moisture at the face.

the destruction of our blacksmith shop
and considerable portion of it's con-

about 12 O. clock, while the night shift
was on duty. The cause of the fire is
unknown, but it was probably due to
the igniting of waste from candle
snuff left by one of the men. The loss
will not exceed $500.


The regular meeting of the stock
holders of the company will be held on
Monday, July 6, 1908, at 2 o'clock p. m.


Respectfully submitted,


JAS. JAY WRIGHT,


Asst Secy.

from Thomasville this evening and placed

This evening the Postmasters' Association rendered a formal reception to the National Organization. The special guests of the evening were Governor Bates and wife.

The great three-compartment raise of the Gem mine was begun in December, 1902, which time the work has been steadily pursued with scarcely any interruption. Part of the undertaking was done under contract for raising 1000 feet.

The raise as completed is 1850 feet in length, inclination 50 degrees, connecting with the main shaft at the depth of 900 feet thus making total length for the shaft of 1850 feet.

It is noteworthy that in this stupendous undertaking no lives have been lost, and no serious accident occurred. This is certainly very fortunate, as in the most carefully conducted mine operations accidents are expected. Mining is perilous and although the experienced miner is of necessity always on the lookout for caving rock and other incidents, he will sometimes get caught.

The difficulty of raising 1850 feet through solid rock can only be properly appreciated by those who have been there and carried out such undertakings.

There is the ventilation to be looked after; skill in timbering to be employed to withstand the shock and weight of the falling rock; the power drills have to be hauled up and down for each day's work, beside the countless other details that enter into the task. There is also the cost to be considered, but with the trained mine manager cost is simply the means to an end and always has to be met before the best results are attained. By this, it is not to be understood that wasteful extravaganza is to be considered as excusable in any case.

In the case of the Gem upraise, great credit is due to the management for the conception of the undertaking and the successful issue. The work has been, as we stated, steadily pursued since the first drill was set at work. No matter what the outlook from the viewpoint of ore, the object was always kept in view, and the first ventilating shaft for the great sluice bore is about completed.

Not only that, we are given to understand that the putting through of this raise has opened a body of ore that is sufficient in size to keep all the present mills of Idaho Springs busy during a generation, and that means a great deal. The completion of the Gem upraise opens vistas of operation for the Consolidated Gem properties that is inimitable in its possibilities. A slight conception of this can only be arrived at by those acquainted with the various holdings of the company. When Mr. Renshaw was acquiring all the various mines on both sides of Gibson gulch, he was forming a consolidation of producers that separately had an enviable record but as a harmonious whole and susceptible of being operated through one thoroughfare, as will ultimately be the case. It would be among the big producers of ore in the world. That he had in mind at the time the connection of the Gem shaft with the tunnel, there is no reasonable doubt, and it is now clear that this is only the beginning of the work of connecting all those properties.

At the collar of the Gem shaft there is one of the finest electrical hoists in the state, capable of sending the shaft another 1000 feet deeper than the tunnel level. It is not probable that any sinking will be necessary for years to come, but that, of course, will depend upon what will be uncovered at that level in the various members of the group. Should there be rich pay ore found at that level necessitating a miner fashion to get at it, the hoist is already in place to start the work at a moment's notice.

It will take some time to place the raise in the shape for performing all the duties required. Levels will have to be started at regular distances, and part of the raise will be set apart for a mammoth ore chute down which will pour the produce of the different properties. By next spring everything should be in fine working order in the mine, and the 1000 ton mill cannot be built too soon.

The reason why he never receives his rightful title of third clerk is obvious.

Meantime he was a happy and lucky sort of lad who was liked by every one from the captain down to the negro deck hands, more commonly known as "rousters."

bad enough if, say, that the appropriation

through poverty. It is no disgrace to
be poor, and there is no use in pretending to be rich when one is poor. But

a poverty-stricken State. It is one of
the richest States in the Union, and is
saic her day than ever before in its history. The State may be a little pressed

of taxation, but to say that Virginia is

antly able to do so, and it would be a
misrepresentation for the statement to
go out that she is not. The Jamestown Exposition Company is

priation be made in installments; and we
hope that some satisfactory arrangement
will be made by which the company can
get an appropriation, for it is only
through an appropriation that it can have
the stamp of the State's approval upon
it.

GINIA, and Virginia must not only own
its child, but give it a comfortable dot.

they will then carry into the next crop
the mycellium that has been the cause
of the rot this year. Potato rot begins
in the form of blight in the field. Later
it shows itself in the tubers stored in
the cellar. Ignorance regarding this
has kept many a farm infected from
year to year, as the farmer has carried
over infected seed from n year to
another. When rot has appeared
therefore, the only thing to do is to
get rid of the potatoes before they
have begun to show the disease. II
the rot is very bad, it will pay better
to feed the smallest Of the tubers to
stock rather than run the risk OF hay
ing them all rot in the bins. In the
ordinary cellar it is rather difficult to
keep potatoes of any kind, much less
those with the rot mycellium con
cealed within. In cold storage where
the temperature is kept at near the
freezing point there is less danger in
trying to hold them for some months
In the ordinary cellar the temperature
frequently goes up to near the sew
enties on warm winter days, and this
is especially so now that many farm
houses are heated by furnaces.-Farm
ers' Review.

Emperor William explained some of the French experiments with double turrets, in which sheep in one turret were killed by the shock of the gun fire in the other.

"That," said the captain, "was due to the shortness of the guns which the French experimenters used. The long guns of the Kearsarge change the field of the highest conclusion."

Captain Hemphill's ready and lucid explanations caused his majesty to say later to an American visitor on the Kearsarge, "A man who knew his business."

In calling the attention of one of the members of his suite to Captain Hemphill's services on the Monitor when she first went into action and to some other fierce naval combats of the civil war, the emperor added:

"Those men are gods to us."

In the Coming Tower.

His majesty also said that the conning tower was the most roomy he had ever been in. With the telephone and signal apparatus in every part of the ship the emperor was naturally interested, and he pointed out one or two good new things. The German constructors have been having some trouble with electrical connections and he was especially interested in them. At present the Kearsarge's general electrical system is invisible, as it is enclosed in semi-permanent constructions.

While the emperor was inspecting the men's quarters he conversed with several of the bluejackets and sailors. He asked one old hand how long he had been in the service. The sailor replied:

"Twenty years, sir."

"That is long enough to be an admiral," said the emperor.

Ease in the Cabin.

When his majesty's inspection of the Kearsarge was finished the party went to the admiral's cabin, and the emperor, seeing a large rocking chair, exclaimed:

"What is this for?"

"For emperors," replied Admiral Cotton.

"Then I will take it," said Emperor William. Some bottles of champagne were then opened.

After a quarter of an hour's general talk the emperor left the battleship, and Admiral Cotton assembled the entire ship's company and addressed them as follows:

Pleased With What He Saw.

"The emperor has inspected the ship quickly, but very thoroughly. His majesty is a judge of all technical matters. He expresses himself as greatly pleased with what he saw. I thank the officers and crew of the Kearsarge for the condition of the ship. I hope every man here will remember that he is a representative of the United States and that he will conduct himself in such manner as to bring credit upon his country and mission. We are here by orders of the president. It is our duty to do all in our power to preserve the feeling of friendship and cordiality between the United States and Germany. Three cheers for his majesty, the emperor!"

The 200 officers and men of the Kearsarge thereupon gave three hearty cheers for Emperor Wilhelm.

Science, he said, teaches us that liquor has no useful service among mankind, but, rather, degrades the citizenship of the country and depletes the public funds, and he wanted to know if it was good policy of business to continue the recognition of an evil that had such an effect on the public welfare. Guthrie Center Oct. 1.—The republican campaign was opened here this afternoon, when Hon. John J. Webster addressed a large audience. He devoted considerable attention to the trust question and was frequently interrupted with applause. He said in part:


The democratic party charges that the republican tariff system fosters monopolies and is the father of trusts. To get rid of these evils it would abolish the tariff on every article that enters into the production of these corporations, even if it should work financial ruin to hundreds of thousands of people engaged in like industries.


The republican party is willing to take off the duty where it will strike a blow at monopoly and benefit the people. It struck such a blow at the coal monopoly, and it will continue to strike such blows wherever circumstances justify it.


The republican party is as much opposed as is the democratic party to unlawful combinations of capital whether formed for the purpose of creating oppressive monopolies, or under the guise of trusts exacting from the people unjust tribute to enable them to pay dividends upon fictitious capitalization of stock.


But the republican party is not opposed to the combination of energies, whether it be in the form of muscle, brain or capital, when used for proper purposes and for the accomplishment of legitimate ends. The republican party understands that the combined efforts of one hundred working men, working together tremendously and in unity, applying their different capabilities and skill to the making of the separate parts of single manufactured article, and by the use of improved and expensive machinery will produce a more valuable output than will the same number of men working separately and in their individual capacities.


The republican party understands that to reach the best results there must be a combination of capital so that advantage may be taken of the lessened cost of production, the cost of transportation, the economizing of unnecessary expenses, and to produce and have on hand a sufficient quantity of the manufactured product to meet the increased demands at home and go into competition with other nations in the markets of the world.


It do not object to a combination of capital for the producing of agricultural machinery simply because it may thereby be able to send its plows and harrows to the farmers of far-off Australia.


It do not object to the combination of capital among contractors for the building of steel structures simply because they are thereby enabled to build bridges over the branches of the Nile in far-off Africa.


It do not object to the combination of capital for the building of railway cars simply because after the demand at home is supplied they send the surplus to the countries of Europe.


It do not object to the combination of capital for the building of locomotives simply because in the year 1899 they sent abroad 517 railway engines to countries upon the continents of Asia and Finland and Denmark and Italy and Algiers and China.


It do not object to Rockefeller's combination of capital simply because the Standard Oil Company owns its own tanks and oil cars, nor because it transports oil in its own ships across the Atlantic ocean, and has its warehouses at Amsterdam.


It do not object because American combination of capital has enabled American producers to send American manufactured goods of one sort or another into all the ports of all the nations of the eastern and western and southern continents.


But we must draw the line somewhere. Raleigh, N. C., June 10.--James Wilcox, the murderer of Nellie Cropsey of Elizabeth City, will have to serve his sentence of thirty years in the state prison here.


He was tried twice. The first time he was convicted of murder in the first degree and sentenced to be hanged. He was given a new trial by the Supreme Court because the spectators at the trial made a demonstration when Wilcox's lawyer arose to speak.

The defendant's attorneys urged that Wilcox should have been given a new trial because first, that most of the evidence was sufficient to have been submitted to the jury; second, that the suicide theory was as reasonable as any other theory.

This line of thought has been strongly pressed upon us by the defendant's able and zealous counsel. To the adoption of this view there are several serious difficulties. There can be no doubt that the deceased was greatly grieved and distressed by the conduct of the defendant; that her affections were trifled with. Her conduct showed her to be a young woman of deep and strong feeling.


The testimony shows that the condition of the river at and near to the front of the Cropsey residence, with its receding shores, is such as to make it necessary for her, if drowned there, to go out seventy-five feet from the shore before reaching water four feet deep. The testimony in respect to the river will conflict with the theory that she could have thrown herself in the water.


In conclusion the opinion says:


"We think that in this case, measured by the standards prescribed by law, the evidence was properly submitted to the jury, and we cannot say they have reached an incorrect conclusion."

Missoula, Mont., June 10.—Carl Dowdell and
Miss Bessie Young were married last evening.
Dowdell, it will be remembered, was the central
figure in sensational cutting affair several
months ago, when J. L. Young, father of the
bride, called him to his room and almost dis

preceded by charge that Dowdell had ruined

along taken sides with her husband against her

programmes of the Maennerchor always in
clude good music which is not hackneyed,
and this one was no exception. The chorus
numbers, under the able direction of Franz

der, it was only by one second that

racy."—Philadelphia Record.

The negro housewife in the West
Indian jungle finds housekeeping very
easy. Fruit and vegetables grow wild
all about the hut, and the river
abounds with fish.


On wash day all she has to do Is
to pick few of the berries of the
soapberry tree, take her clothes to
the river, and use berries as she
would use ordinary soap. Even her
cooking pots grow on the trees, the
calabash cut in halves being used for
this purpose. Calabashes are used
also for bowls, basins and jugs for
carrying water from the river, while
the small ones make excellent cups.


In the afternoon, when she is ready
for her cup of tea, the negress picks
half a dozen leaves from the lane
bush growing at her door, boils them.
squeezes the juice from a sugarcane
for sweetening, and the cocoanut sup
plies the milk. Thus she has a de-
liclous cup of tea without depending
ON the grocer for it.


She makes the mats for her floor
out of the dried leaves of the banana,
plated and sewn together, as the old
country people in this country make
their rag mats.
